about_blocks.text: About Neurosync Brain Treatment Centre in Woodbridge
about_blocks.html: About Neurosync Brain Treatment Centre in Woodbridge

about_blocks.text: Neurosync Brain Treatment Centre is a private outpatient clinic in Woodbridge, in the City of Vaughan, that offers brain stimulation treatments. Its main service is MeRT, short for Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy, which the clinic describes as a personalized form of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). It offers standard rTMS too. The clinic says it opened in 2023 and works from a unit at 3530 Rutherford Road, open Monday to Friday from 9am to 5pm. There are no beds, overnight stays or detox services.

The clinic says it opened in 2023 and works from a unit at 3530 Rutherford Road, open Monday to Friday from 9am to 5pm. There are no beds, overnight stays or detox services.

about_blocks.text: Most of the clinic's website is about autism. It offers MeRT to children with autism spectrum disorder aged four and older, and it also lists depression, anxiety, PTSD, traumatic brain injury, concussion and sleep problems among the concerns it assesses. Its rTMS page adds conditions such as OCD, migraines, chronic pain and substance abuse. The site does not describe addiction counselling, withdrawal management or a structured recovery program.

about_blocks.text: Treatment starts with an evaluation of about 45 minutes, which includes a short eyes-closed brainwave recording (qEEG) and a heart recording (EKG), plus a review of health history and medications. The clinic says the recording is processed on Wave Neuroscience's platform, the company behind MeRT, and a stimulation protocol is built from the results if the team thinks treatment is suitable. Sessions then run about 30 minutes, five days a week, with repeat recordings during the course to check changes and adjust the protocol.

centre.faq_heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Neurosync Brain Treatment Centre

faqs.question: Is Neurosync Brain Treatment Centre a residential rehab?

answer_blocks.text: No. Neurosync is an outpatient clinic in Woodbridge, Vaughan, open Monday to Friday from 9am to 5pm, and you go home after each session. It has no beds, overnight stays or detox. If you need live-in addiction treatment or medically supervised withdrawal, look at residential centres in the GTA and across Ontario instead.

faqs.question: Does Neurosync treat drug or alcohol addiction?

answer_blocks.text: Addiction is not the clinic's focus. Its rTMS page lists substance abuse among conditions rTMS may be used for, and its depression page lists fewer cravings for drugs or alcohol as one possible benefit, with the note that results vary and are not guaranteed. The clinic does not describe addiction counselling, detox or a recovery program, so talk with your doctor about pairing any brain stimulation with established addiction care.

faqs.question: What is MeRT, and how is it different from rTMS?

answer_blocks.text: MeRT (Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy) is what the clinic calls a personalized version of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. A magnetic coil placed on the head delivers pulses to chosen areas of the brain. With MeRT, the clinic sets the frequency and location using each person's qEEG brainwave and EKG heart-rate recordings, while standard rTMS usually follows set protocols for a specific diagnosis.

faqs.question: What is the evidence and regulatory status of MeRT?

answer_blocks.text: MeRT is not approved for autism, and there is no large study showing it works better than a placebo for that use. In the United States, TMS devices are approved for some conditions, such as depression, OCD, migraine and smoking cessation, but the FDA has not approved MeRT for autism. Neurosync says its clinicians use FDA-cleared equipment off-label. Los Angeles Times reporting in 2024 and 2025, and an editorial by TMS researchers from UCLA and the US National Institute of Mental Health, described the evidence for autism as very limited. Discuss it with your own doctor before you start.

answer_blocks.text: The clinic does not publish prices, so ask for a written quote for the assessment and the full course. Neurosync states that its services are not covered by OHIP or private insurance. It says funding is available through the Ontario Autism Program, which may apply to eligible children with autism.

faqs.question: How long does a course of treatment last?

answer_blocks.text: Sessions take about 30 minutes and run five days a week. The clinic says treatment often begins with a two-week assessment period of nine sessions, followed by a repeat brainwave recording. Its website gives about one month of daily sessions in one place and recommends six to eight weeks for many plans in another, so ask what it suggests for you.

faqs.question: What happens at the first appointment?

answer_blocks.text: The first visit is an evaluation of about 45 minutes. You complete new-patient forms, go over your symptoms, medications and health history, and have a 10-minute eyes-closed qEEG and an EKG. After the data is analyzed, the team discusses the findings and only offers a treatment protocol if it thinks MeRT is suitable.

faqs.question: What side effects does the clinic mention?

answer_blocks.text: The clinic lists headache, scalp discomfort, tingling, facial muscle twitching and lightheadedness, which it says are usually mild and short-lived. It names seizures as a rare risk with TMS-based treatment. It reviews medications, seizure history and any implanted metal or electronic devices before treatment, since these can affect suitability.

faqs.question: Where is Neurosync Brain Treatment Centre?

answer_blocks.text: The clinic is at 3530 Rutherford Road, Unit 76, in Woodbridge, Vaughan (L4L 1A6), in York Region just north of Toronto. Rutherford Road connects to Highway 400, so it is about 35 to 45 minutes by car from downtown Toronto and about 20 to 30 minutes from Brampton, Richmond Hill or Mississauga, depending on traffic. Call 905-758-9885 to book.
